tips.title: Auxin: shoots towards, roots away
tips.body: Auxin gathers on the **shaded** side. In a **shoot** it makes cells **elongate**, so the shoot bends towards the light. In a **root** it **inhibits** elongation, so the root bends the other way. Same hormone, opposite effect.

tips.title: Two kinds of defence only
tips.body: Edexcel names **physical** barriers, such as the waxy cuticle and cell walls, and **chemical** defences, such as poisons. There is no third category to reach for.

tips.title: Say elongation, not just growth
tips.body: "The shoot grows towards the light" describes what happens. The mark is the mechanism: auxin accumulates on the shaded side, cells there **elongate more**, so the shoot bends.

tips.title: Say which side, then which way
tips.body: For any tropism, answer in two steps: **auxin collects on the shaded or lower side**, then **what that side does**. In a shoot it **elongates**, so the shoot bends **towards** the light. Naming the side first makes the direction follow instead of being guessed.

why.matters:
A plant cannot run away, cannot look for water and cannot hide. Everything it does about a problem it does by **growing differently**, or by chemistry.

That is why this topic pairs three things that look unrelated. Adaptations are what growing differently looks like over generations; defences are the chemistry; and hormones are how a plant with no nervous system still responds to where the light is and which way is up — within days rather than generations.

examples.title: Why a cactus has spines instead of leaves
examples.body:
A leaf is a device for losing water, which is fine when there is water. In a desert it is fatal, so a cactus has traded the leaf away: the spines **are** its leaves, reduced until they have almost no surface at all.

Photosynthesis moves to the swollen green **stem**, which also stores the water. A thick waxy cuticle cuts losses further, the roots spread wide and shallow to catch any rain that falls, and the spines happen to make the plant difficult to eat. Every one of those is the same problem solved five times.

boxes.title: Spines, not leaves
boxes.body: Almost no surface, so almost no loss.

boxes.title: Wide shallow roots
boxes.body: Catch rain the moment it falls.

visual.alt: Four boxes round a centre reading keep the water in: spines instead of leaves, a swollen stem that photosynthesises and stores water, a thick waxy cuticle, and wide shallow roots

examples.title: Why a plant on a windowsill leans
examples.body:
Leave a seedling by a window and within days it is bending towards the light. No eye or nerve is involved: the shoot tip detects the direction of the light, and **auxin**, a growth hormone made at the tip, collects on the **shaded** side of the shoot.

Auxin makes shoot cells **elongate**, so the shaded side grows longer than the lit side and the stem bends towards the light — which is where the leaves are wanted. Turn the pot round and it bends back. The same hormone in a **root** has the opposite effect, slowing growth, which is why a root bends downwards with the same chemistry.

nodes.text: The shoot bends to the light

visual.alt: A flow chart of phototropism: light from one side makes auxin gather on the shaded side of the shoot, those cells elongate, and the shoot bends towards the light

examples.title: Why a banana ripens the fruit next to it
examples.body:
Put an unripe avocado in a paper bag with a ripe banana and it ripens in a day or two. The banana is giving off **ethene**, a hormone that is a gas, and the bag keeps it around the fruit instead of letting it drift off.

Ethene triggers ripening — starch to sugar, firm to soft — and because it is a gas it spreads from fruit to fruit, which is what *one bad apple* is about. It is also why fruit is shipped unripe and ripened on arrival in rooms dosed with ethene, and why bananas are kept away from everything else in a fruit bowl.

visual.alt: A flow chart of fruit ripening: a ripe banana gives off ethene gas, and if the fruit is kept together in a bag the gas stays around it and ripens the fruit beside it, while in the open it drifts away

steps.title: Surviving extremes
steps.body:
This whole topic is **Biology only** (5.9B, 5.10B, 6.14B to 6.16B).

Plants cannot move, so they adapt. In a **desert** the enemy is water loss: cacti have **spines** instead of leaves (tiny surface area), a **thick waxy cuticle**, stems that **store water**, and long or spreading **roots**. In a **waterlogged** swamp the problem is oxygen for the roots: mangroves and rice have **air spaces** running down to the roots, or roots that grow up out of the water. On a **sand dune** marram grass **rolls its leaves** to trap humid air around its stomata. Stomata are adapted too: desert plants have **fewer** of them, often only on the lower surface, and they are **sunk into pits** where humid air collects so the water vapour gradient stays small. Some open their stomata only at **night**, when the air is cooler and less water is lost. Every adaptation is explained by the same ideas: surface area, the water vapour gradient, and what the roots need.

steps.title: Defending against pests and pathogens
steps.body:
Plants are food for animals and hosts for microbes, and they fight back.

- **Physical defences**: **thorns** and **spines**, **hairy** leaves, a thick **waxy cuticle**, and **bark** or a **cellulose cell wall** that pathogens must get through.
- **Chemical defences**: **poisons** that make the plant taste bad or harm the animal (foxglove, deadly nightshade), and **antibacterial** or **antifungal** chemicals (mint, witch hazel). Some plants release chemicals that **attract the predators** of the insect eating them.
- **From defence to medicine**: chemicals plants make to defend themselves are where many drugs came from. Aspirin came from salicin in willow bark, which the body turns into salicylic acid; digoxin for heart failure comes from the foxglove, quinine for malaria comes from cinchona bark, and artemisinin, also for malaria, comes from sweet wormwood. The plant makes them to poison or deter pests; we use them at a controlled dose.

steps.text: Rose thorns: physical, a barrier that stops animals biting
Nettle sting: chemical, a toxin delivered by a hair
Thick bark on a tree: physical, pathogens cannot get through
Mint oil: chemical, antibacterial

check.solution: Poisons are chemicals; thorns, bark and hairs are physical barriers.

steps.title: Auxin: growing towards the light
steps.body: Plants respond to their surroundings with **hormones**. **Auxin** is made in the **tips** of shoots and roots and controls **cell elongation**. In a shoot lit from one side, auxin builds up on the **shaded** side, those cells grow longer, and the shoot **bends towards the light**: **positive phototropism**. Cover the tip and the shoot grows straight up, because the tip is where light is sensed. Remove the tip and the shoot stops growing and does not bend, because the tip is where the auxin is made.

visuals.problem: Classic experiment: a shoot tip is removed, then a block of agar that had touched the tip is placed on the cut end, off to one side

steps.text: The shoot bends away from the side with the agar block
Something in the tip has passed into the agar and made the cells under it grow longer
That something is auxin, and it works even without light

check.prompt: In a shoot lit from the left, where does auxin build up and what happens?
check.solution: Auxin collects on the shaded side and makes it grow faster.

markScheme.description: Shaded side elongates, bends to light

options: In the roots, so the shoot stops growing
Evenly on both sides, so the shoot grows straight
On the left, lit side; those cells elongate and the shoot bends right
On the right, shaded side; those cells elongate and the shoot bends left, towards the light

steps.title: Auxin in roots: the opposite effect
steps.body: The same hormone does the **opposite** in roots: a high concentration of auxin **inhibits** elongation. Lay a seedling on its side. Auxin settles on the **lower** side of both shoot and root. In the shoot the lower cells grow faster and it bends **up** (negative gravitropism). In the root the lower cells grow **less** and it bends **down** (positive gravitropism). One hormone, two tissues, two responses.

visuals.problem: A root lying sideways: explain why it bends down

steps.text: Auxin collects on the lower side of the root
In roots, auxin inhibits elongation, so the lower cells grow less than the upper cells
The upper side grows faster, so the root curves downwards into the soil

check.prompt: Why do shoots and roots of a seedling lying on its side bend in opposite directions?
check.solution: Same distribution of auxin, opposite response in the two tissues.

markScheme.description: Stimulates in shoot, inhibits in root

options: Auxin collects on different sides in the shoot and the root, because gravity pulls it up in one and down in the other
Light reaches the shoot but not the root, so the shoot bends towards it while the root responds to gravity
Auxin collects on the lower side of both, but stimulates elongation in the shoot and inhibits it in the root
Only the shoot contains auxin, so the root grows straight down under its own weight while the shoot bends

steps.title: Your turn: investigating phototropism
steps.body:
Plan an investigation into phototropism. You have cress seedlings in pots, three cardboard boxes and a lamp.

- **Independent variable**: the light the seedlings get. One box with a slit on one side, one with a hole in the top, one fully closed (no light at all).
- **Dependent variable**: the angle the shoots bend, measured with a protractor after three days, and the height of each shoot, measured with a ruler. The closed box is told apart from the top-hole box by height and colour, not by bending.
- **Control variables**: number of seedlings, water, temperature, age of the seedlings, and for the two lit boxes the same lamp at the same distance.
- **Repeats**: at least five seedlings per box, and take the mean angle and mean height, so one odd seedling does not decide the result.
- **Control group**: seedlings in the open, lit from above. This checks that the box itself, warmer and more humid, is not what changes the growth.

Predict each result and explain it with where the auxin collects.

visuals.problem: Predict and explain the three boxes

steps.text: Slit on one side: shoots bend towards the slit, because auxin collects on the shaded side and those cells elongate
Hole in the top: shoots grow straight up, because light reaches both sides equally and auxin is spread evenly
Fully closed: shoots grow straight but tall, pale and spindly, because with no light to respond to the auxin is evenly spread and the seedlings keep elongating in search of light

check.prompt: In this investigation, what is the dependent variable?
check.solution: You change the direction of the light and measure how far the shoots bend.

markScheme.description: Angle of bending

options: The number of seedlings planted in each of the pots
The angle the shoots bend, measured with a protractor
The direction the light comes from, set by the box
The temperature of the room where the boxes are kept

steps.title: Going deeper: unfamiliar plants, familiar reasons
steps.body:
Examiners invent plants. A leaf that folds up at midday, a root with air channels, a seed that only germinates after a fire. You are not expected to know the plant; you are expected to reason from **surface area**, the **water vapour gradient**, **oxygen for respiration**, and the **hormones**. Say what the feature does, then what problem it solves.

For hormones, be precise about **where** auxin is made (the tip), **where** it collects (the shaded or lower side), and **what** it does (elongation in shoots, inhibition in roots). To evaluate a commercial use, give a benefit, a drawback and a judgement.

visuals.problem: Seeds of some plants only germinate after heating by a fire. Suggest an advantage.

steps.text: After a fire the ground is clear of competing plants and rich in ash minerals
Seedlings that appear then have light, space and nutrients
Germinating earlier, under a dense canopy, would waste the seed

check.prompt: A plant closes its stomata at midday in hot weather. What is the trade-off?
check.solution: Closed stomata stop water leaving and stop carbon dioxide entering.

markScheme.description: Water saved, photosynthesis slowed

options: It loses more water through the cuticle, but the leaf stays cooler in the sun
It saves water but takes in less carbon dioxide, so photosynthesis slows
It saves water and takes in more carbon dioxide, so photosynthesis speeds up
There is no trade-off, because closed stomata still let carbon dioxide through

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Extreme environments: cacti reduce water loss (spines, thick cuticle, water storage); swamp plants get oxygen to roots (air spaces); marram grass rolls its leaves.
- Defences: physical (thorns, hairs, cuticle, bark) and chemical (poisons, antibacterial chemicals, attracting predators of pests).
- Auxin: made in tips; shoots bend towards light because the shaded side elongates; in roots it inhibits elongation, so roots bend down.
- Gibberellins: germination, flowering, bigger fruit. Ethene: ripening.
- Uses: selective weedkillers and rooting powder (auxin), seedless and larger fruit (gibberellin), ripening on demand (ethene).
- Some plant defence chemicals became medicines: aspirin (willow bark), digoxin (foxglove), quinine (cinchona), artemisinin (sweet wormwood).

steps.text: Why do shoots bend to light? Auxin on the shaded side makes those cells elongate
Why do roots bend down? Auxin on the lower side inhibits elongation there
Why is fruit shipped green? Ethene ripens it on demand at the shop

questions.prompt: Explain how auxin makes a shoot bend towards the light.
questions.solution: Three links: where auxin is made, where it collects, and what it does to the cells.

Light causes auxin to build up on the shaded side

Auxin makes shoot cells elongate, so the shaded side grows faster than the lit side, and the shoot bends towards the light. This response is called positive phototropism.

questions.prompt: In roots, auxin has the opposite effect to shoots. What does a high concentration of auxin do in a root?
questions.solution: Same hormone, opposite response. In a root lying on its side, auxin collects on the lower side, that side grows less, and the root bends downwards.

It has no effect in roots at all, so a root always grows straight whatever the conditions
It makes the root grow towards the light, so the root turns and grows up out of the soil
It inhibits cell elongation, so the side where auxin collects grows less and the root bends towards it

questions.prompt: Gibberellins are used commercially to
questions.solution: Gibberellins trigger germination and flowering and increase fruit size.

markScheme.description: Germination, flowering, fruit size

questions.prompt: Marram grass grows on sand dunes, where the sand holds little water and the wind is strong. Its leaves are rolled into a tube with the stomata on the inside, and it has hairs on the inner surface and a thick cuticle on the outside. Explain how these features help it survive.
questions.solution: Level-marked. Each feature should be linked to the water vapour gradient or to evaporation.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two relevant points about features that reduce transpiration in a dry, windy place, not linked
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a mostly correct account of features that reduce transpiration in a dry, windy place with some links
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, complete account of features that reduce transpiration in a dry, windy place using the correct terms

criteria.text: Rolling the leaf traps humid air inside next to the stomata
So the water vapour gradient is small and less water diffuses out
Hairs also trap moist air and reduce air movement across the stomata
The thick cuticle on the outer surface is waterproof, so water is not lost through the exposed side
Stomata on the inside are sheltered from the wind, which would otherwise blow away humid air and speed up transpiration
Together these reduce transpiration so the plant can survive where water is scarce

questions.modelAnswer: Marram grass lives where water is scarce and wind would drive transpiration fast. Rolling the leaf puts the stomata on the inside, where the trapped air becomes humid, so the concentration gradient of water vapour between leaf and air is small and diffusion out is slow. The hairs trap more moist air and stop the wind moving air across the stomata, which would otherwise keep the gradient steep. The thick waxy cuticle on the outside is waterproof, so the exposed surface loses almost nothing. Every feature reduces transpiration, so the plant keeps enough water to survive on the dune.

questions.prompt: Plants growing in waterlogged soil often have air spaces running down their roots. What is the most likely reason?
questions.solution: Roots respire and need oxygen. Underwater, the only source is air brought down inside the plant.

markScheme.description: Oxygen for root respiration

options: Root cells need oxygen for respiration, and waterlogged soil holds little oxygen, so air spaces carry oxygen from the shoot down to the roots
Air spaces let light reach the root cells, so the roots can photosynthesise underwater where the soil does not block the light
Air spaces make the roots lighter, so the plant floats higher in the water and its leaves stay above the surface in the light
Air spaces store water for dry periods, so the plant can survive when the swamp dries out in summer and the roots are exposed

questions.prompt: Selective weedkillers contain synthetic auxin. Why do they kill broad-leaved weeds in a lawn but not the grass?
questions.solution: Synthetic auxin makes the weeds grow so fast and unevenly that they die. Grasses respond far less, so the lawn survives.

markScheme.description: Weeds respond with uncontrolled growth; grass is less sensitive

options: The weedkiller only lands on tall plants, because the spray is applied above the height of the grass, so the short grass underneath is never touched by it
Grasses have no auxin receptors of any kind, so synthetic auxin cannot enter their cells, while broad-leaved plants absorb it through their large leaf surface
Broad-leaved plants absorb more of the hormone and respond to it with uncontrolled growth that kills them, while narrow-leaved grasses are much less affected
Grass is not a flowering plant, so it does not make or respond to plant hormones, while broad-leaved weeds are flowering plants that use auxin to grow

questions.prompt: A grower wants to produce seedless grapes, and also to make them larger. Explain how a plant hormone could be used, and give one possible drawback of using hormones in this way.
questions.solution: Two uses named with the right hormone, then a drawback that is specific.

markScheme.description: Seedless fruit with gibberellin
Larger fruit with gibberellin
A specific drawback

criteria.text: Gibberellins applied to the flowers make fruit develop without fertilisation, so there are no seeds
Gibberellins make the fruit grow larger
Drawback: cost, or the treated fruit cannot be grown from seed, or possible effects on the environment or consumer concern

questions.modelAnswer: Spraying the unpollinated flowers with gibberellin makes the fruit develop without fertilisation, so the grapes form without seeds. Applying gibberellins also makes the fruits grow larger. A drawback is that the hormones cost money and time to apply, the treated plants produce no seed for the next crop, and some consumers are uneasy about fruit produced this way.

questions.prompt: Bananas are picked green and shipped unripe, then exposed to ethene before sale. Why is this better than shipping ripe bananas?
questions.solution: Ethene lets the ripening be switched on at the right moment.

markScheme.description: Firmer in transport, ripening on demand

options: Ripe bananas cannot be transported at all, because the ethene they release would damage the ship's refrigeration
Ethene makes the bananas grow bigger on the ship, so more fruit arrives at the shop than was picked from the plants
Green bananas contain more sugar than ripe ones, so they are sweeter by the time they have been treated with ethene
Unripe fruit is firmer and lasts longer in transport, and ripening can be timed to when the fruit reaches the shop

questions.prompt: Some plants release chemicals that attract wasps which lay eggs inside caterpillars eating the plant. Explain how this defends the plant and why it counts as a chemical defence.
questions.solution: Say how the pest is reduced, and why "chemical" is the right label.

markScheme.description: Predator kills the pests
Indirect defence
A substance the plant makes, not a barrier

criteria.text: The wasp larvae kill the caterpillars, so fewer leaves are eaten
The plant does not attack the pest directly; it produces a substance that brings in a predator of the pest
It is chemical because the defence is a substance the plant makes, not a physical barrier

questions.modelAnswer: The chemical brings in wasps whose larvae kill the caterpillars, so the pest population falls and less of the plant is eaten. The plant defends itself indirectly, by recruiting a predator of its pest. It is a chemical defence because it works through a substance the plant produces, unlike thorns or a thick cuticle, which are physical barriers.

questions.prompt: A root growing sideways bends downwards. Auxin collects on the lower side of the root. What effect does auxin have on the cells on the lower side?
questions.solution: In roots auxin **inhibits their elongation**. The lower side grows less than the upper side, so the root bends down: positive gravitropism. In a shoot the same auxin makes cells elongate faster.

markScheme.description: inhibits their elongation

options: makes them elongate faster
inhibits their elongation
makes them divide faster
has no effect on them at all

questions.prompt: Which structure is a physical barrier that a pathogen must get through to enter a plant cell?
questions.solution: **The cell wall**: a tough layer of cellulose outside the cell membrane that a pathogen must break through. The vacuole, nucleus and chloroplasts are inside the cell.

markScheme.description: the cell wall

options: the vacuole
the nucleus
the cell wall
the chloroplast

questions.prompt: A seedling is laid on its side in the dark. Auxin collects on the lower side of the shoot. What happens to the shoot?
questions.solution: In a shoot auxin stimulates elongation, so **the lower side elongates more, so the shoot bends upwards**: negative gravitropism. In a root the same auxin inhibits elongation, so the root bends down.

markScheme.description: The lower side elongates more, so the shoot bends upwards

options: The lower side elongates less, so the shoot bends downwards
The lower side elongates more, so the shoot bends upwards
Both sides elongate equally, so the shoot keeps growing sideways
The upper side elongates more, so the shoot bends downwards

questions.prompt: Many desert plants have small or needle-shaped leaves. How does this help them survive?
questions.solution: **A smaller surface area means less water is lost by transpiration**. The cost is less surface to absorb light, which is why many cacti photosynthesise in their green stems instead.

markScheme.description: A smaller surface area means less water is lost by transpiration

options: Small leaves absorb more light, so photosynthesis is faster in the desert sun
Small leaves hold more stomata, so the plant takes in more carbon dioxide
Small leaves store more water inside them, so the plant survives drought
A smaller surface area means less water is lost by transpiration

questions.prompt: A desert plant has its stomata sunk in pits below the leaf surface, with hairs around each opening. How does this reduce water loss?
questions.solution: Water vapour leaving the stoma collects in the still air of the pit, where the wind cannot blow it away. **Humid air is trapped in the pit, so the water vapour gradient is smaller**, and less water diffuses out. The stomata can still open to let carbon dioxide in.

markScheme.description: Humid air is trapped in the pit, so the water vapour gradient is smaller

options: The pits collect rainwater, which the stomata absorb back into the leaf
The pits keep the stomata permanently closed, so no water vapour escapes
Humid air is trapped in the pit, so the water vapour gradient is smaller
The hairs absorb the water vapour before it can leave the stomata

questions.prompt: In which part of a growing shoot is the hormone auxin produced?
questions.solution: **The tip of the shoot.** Auxin is made in the growing tip and moves down into the cells behind it, where it makes them elongate. That is why a shoot whose tip has been cut off, or covered with a light-proof cap, no longer bends towards the light: the part that makes the auxin and detects the light has gone or is in the dark. The roots make their own auxin at their tips, but the question asks about a shoot; the leaves and flowers do not control the shoot's growth.

markScheme.description: the tip of the shoot

options: The fully grown leaves
The flower buds
The tip of the shoot
The base of the stem

questions.prompt: Many plants make bitter or poisonous chemicals. Some of these chemicals are used as medicines: for example quinine, from the bark of the cinchona tree, is used to treat malaria. What is the function of these chemicals for the plant itself?
questions.solution: **They defend the plant against pests and pathogens.** A plant cannot run away or fight, so many plants make chemicals that poison or deter the insects and grazing animals that eat them, or that kill the bacteria and fungi that infect them. Because a chemical that kills a plant's pathogens or pests can sometimes kill a human pathogen too, or act on human cells in a useful way, several of these defence chemicals have become medicines: quinine against the malaria protist, and aspirin, developed from a chemical in willow bark, to relieve pain. The chemicals are not pollinator attractants, food reserves (that is starch) or waterproofing (that is the waxy cuticle).

markScheme.description: they defend the plant against pests and pathogens

options: They attract insects that carry pollen between the plant's flowers
They defend the plant against pests and pathogens that attack it
They are the plant's store of energy for growth in the spring
They form a waterproof layer that stops the leaves drying out

questions.prompt: A grower wants a batch of flowering plants to produce their flowers earlier than they naturally would, so that they are in bloom in time for a spring festival. Which treatment is most likely to work?
questions.skill: choosing a hormone for flower formation
questions.solution: **Spray the plants with gibberellins.** Gibberellins are the plant hormones that promote flower formation, as well as ending seed dormancy, so they are used commercially to bring plants into flower sooner and more evenly, and also to make fruit grow larger or form without seeds. Ethene's commercial use is ripening fruit; it does not make shoots grow taller, and on most cut and pot plants it makes flowers age and drop. Synthetic auxin at a high concentration is a weedkiller: it makes broad-leaved plants grow so fast and so unevenly that they die, so spraying the crop with it would destroy it. Nitrate fertiliser supplies nitrogen for making proteins; plants do not turn it into gibberellins.

markScheme.description: spray with gibberellins, which promote flower formation

options: Spray the plants with gibberellins, the hormones that promote flower formation
Keep the plants in a room filled with ethene gas, which makes the shoots grow taller so they flower sooner
Spray the plants with a strong solution of synthetic auxin, so the shoots grow faster and flower sooner
Water the plants with nitrate fertiliser, which the plants convert into the hormone that controls flowering

questions.prompt: A student cuts the tip off a seedling shoot and places a small block of agar jelly containing auxin on the left-hand side of the cut surface. The seedling is then kept in the dark. What will the shoot do, and why?
questions.skill: predicting growth from an auxin source
questions.solution: **It bends to the right, away from the block.** Auxin makes the cells of a shoot **elongate**. The auxin in the block moves down the left side of the shoot only, so the cells on the left grow longer than those on the right, and the shoot curves away from its longer side: to the right. This is exactly what happens in a shoot lit from one side, where the auxin made in the tip moves to the shaded side and that side grows more, so the shoot bends towards the light. Here the student has supplied the uneven auxin directly, so no light is needed. Auxin does inhibit elongation in **roots**, which is why a root bends the other way, but this is a shoot. A shoot without its tip does not stop growing altogether while auxin is being supplied, and it certainly does not grow straight: the whole point of the block is that the auxin is on one side.

markScheme.description: bends to the right, because auxin makes the cells on the left elongate more

options: It bends to the left, because auxin stops the cells on the left side from elongating, as it does in a root
It bends to the right, because the auxin makes the cells on the left side elongate more than those on the right
It grows straight upwards, because a shoot can only bend when light shines on it from one side
It stops growing completely, because a shoot without its tip cannot respond to auxin from any source

questions.prompt: Name the growth response in which a root grows downwards, in the direction of the pull of gravity.
questions.solution: **Gravitropism**, also called geotropism. A root grows towards the pull of gravity, which is a **positive** gravitropism; a shoot grows away from it, which is negative gravitropism. Both responses are controlled by auxin. In a root lying on its side, auxin collects on the lower side and **inhibits** elongation there, so the upper side grows faster and the root bends down. In a shoot the same build-up on the lower side **stimulates** elongation, so the shoot bends up.

markScheme.description: gravitropism (or geotropism)

questions.prompt: A shop receives two crates, each holding 80 green bananas. One crate is kept for four days in a room containing ethene gas; the other is kept for four days in ordinary air at the same temperature. After the four days, 68 of the bananas kept in ethene are ripe and 24 of the bananas kept in ordinary air are ripe. Calculate the difference between the percentages of bananas that have ripened in the two crates.
questions.skill: percentage ripened with and without ethene
questions.solution: Ethene crate: $\dfrac{68}{80} \times 100 = 85\%$. Ordinary air: $\dfrac{24}{80} \times 100 = 30\%$. Difference $= 85 - 30 = 55$ percentage points. Ethene is the plant hormone that triggers **ripening**. Fruit is picked and transported green, when it is firm and does not bruise, and then exposed to ethene so that it ripens just before it is sold. The 30% in ordinary air ripened because ripening bananas release ethene of their own, which spreads to the fruit around them.

markScheme.description: works out both percentages, 85% and 30%, or divides both counts by 80

questions.prompt: A seedling shoot is 20 mm long. It is lit from one side for three days and bends towards the light. Afterwards the side of the shoot that was in shade measures 32 mm from base to tip and the side that faced the light measures 26 mm. A student says that the shaded side grew about 1.2 times as much as the lit side, because 32 ÷ 26 = 1.23. Calculate how many times greater the increase in length of the shaded side was than the increase in length of the lit side.
questions.skill: comparing growth on the two sides of a bending shoot
questions.solution: Both sides started at 20 mm, so the student should compare the **increases**, not the final lengths. Shaded side: $32 - 20 = 12$ mm of growth. Lit side: $26 - 20 = 6$ mm of growth. So the shaded side grew $\dfrac{12}{6} = 2$ times as much. Dividing the final lengths hides most of the difference, because the original 20 mm is counted in both. The result matches the auxin explanation: auxin made in the tip moves to the **shaded side**, where it makes the cells **elongate** more, so that side becomes longer and the shoot curves towards the light.

markScheme.description: finds the two increases in length: 12 mm and 6 mm
divides the increase on the shaded side by the increase on the lit side

questions.prompt: Describe how the leaf cuticle and the cell wall protect a plant against pathogens, and describe one way in which plants use chemicals to defend themselves.
questions.solution: The **cuticle** is a waxy, waterproof layer over the surface of the leaf. Pathogens such as fungi and bacteria cannot easily penetrate it or get the moisture they need on it, so it is the first **physical barrier** to infection. If a pathogen does get inside the leaf, each cell is surrounded by a tough **cellulose cell wall**, a second barrier it must break through before it can reach the cell contents. Plants also defend themselves with **chemicals**: some make poisons or bitter-tasting substances that deter or kill insects and grazing animals, and some make antibacterial or antifungal chemicals that kill the pathogens that land on them.

markScheme.description: the waxy cuticle is a waterproof layer that pathogens cannot easily penetrate, so it stops them entering the leaf
the tough cellulose cell wall is a barrier a pathogen must break through before it can enter the cell
a chemical defence: poisons or bitter chemicals that deter or kill pests, or antibacterial or antifungal chemicals that kill pathogens

criteria.text: Describes the cuticle as a waxy, waterproof layer on the leaf surface that pathogens cannot easily penetrate, so they are kept out of the leaf
Describes the tough cellulose cell wall as a barrier a pathogen must break through to reach the inside of a cell
Describes a chemical defence: poisons or bitter-tasting chemicals that deter or kill insects and grazing animals, or antibacterial or antifungal chemicals that kill pathogens

questions.modelAnswer: The leaf cuticle is a layer of wax on the outer surface of the leaf. It is waterproof, so water does not sit on the leaf for fungal spores to germinate in, and it is a barrier that bacteria and fungi cannot easily penetrate, so most pathogens never get inside the leaf at all. Any pathogen that does get in, for example through a wound, meets a second physical barrier: every plant cell is surrounded by a tough wall of cellulose, which the pathogen has to break through before it can reach the cell membrane and the contents of the cell. Plants also defend themselves chemically. Many make poisons or bitter-tasting chemicals in their leaves, which deter insects and grazing animals from eating them or kill the insects that do. Others make chemicals that kill bacteria or fungi that land on them. Some of these defence chemicals are useful to people as medicines, such as quinine, which treats malaria, and the chemical in willow bark from which aspirin was developed.

questions.prompt: A plant grows on the floor of a rainforest, where little light reaches it, the air is very humid and rain falls almost every day. It has very large, thin leaves with a thin cuticle and many stomata on both surfaces. Explain how these features suit the plant to its environment.
questions.skill: adaptations to a dim, humid environment
questions.solution: On the forest floor **light** is the factor in short supply, and **water** is not. Very **large leaves** give a large surface area to catch as much as possible of the dim light for photosynthesis, and thin leaves let light reach every cell. A **thin cuticle** costs the plant less to make and lets more light through to the cells, and the plant can afford it because in humid air and with water always available, water loss by transpiration is slow and easily replaced. **Many stomata on both surfaces** let carbon dioxide diffuse into the leaf quickly for photosynthesis; in a desert that would cost a great deal of water, but in humid air the concentration gradient of water vapour out of the leaf is small, so little is lost. The features are the reverse of a desert plant's, because the problem to solve is the reverse.

markScheme.description: large, thin leaves give a large surface area to absorb the little light available for photosynthesis
a thin cuticle is enough because water loss is low in humid air and water is easily replaced from the wet soil
many stomata on both surfaces let carbon dioxide diffuse in quickly for photosynthesis, and the water this loses is not a problem in humid air

criteria.text: Explains that the large, thin leaves give a large surface area to absorb as much as possible of the dim light for photosynthesis
Explains that a thin cuticle is enough because the humid air keeps water loss by transpiration low and the daily rain replaces any water lost
Explains that many stomata on both surfaces let carbon dioxide diffuse in quickly for photosynthesis, and that the extra water loss this allows does not matter in humid air with plentiful water

questions.modelAnswer: A plant on the rainforest floor has the opposite problem to a desert plant. Water is plentiful, because it rains almost every day and the air is humid, but light is scarce, because the trees above take most of it. The very large leaves give the plant a large surface area to absorb as much as possible of the little light that reaches it, and because the leaves are thin, light reaches all the photosynthesising cells. The cuticle is thin because a thick waxy cuticle is a defence against water loss, and here water loss is not a danger: the humid air means there is only a small concentration gradient of water vapour between the inside of the leaf and the air outside, so transpiration is slow, and the wet soil replaces what is lost. A thin cuticle also lets more light through to the cells beneath. The many stomata on both surfaces let carbon dioxide diffuse into the leaf quickly, so that photosynthesis is not limited by a shortage of carbon dioxide on top of the shortage of light. Open stomata lose water vapour, which is why a desert plant has few of them, but on the forest floor the loss is small and easily replaced, so the plant can afford them.

questions.prompt: Devise an investigation to show that it is the tip of a shoot that detects the direction of light, and explain the results you would expect in terms of auxin.
questions.solution: Grow sets of similar seedlings in a box that lets light in from **one side only**. Leave one set with **intact tips**, cover the tips of a second set with **light-proof caps**, and **remove the tips** of a third set; a fourth set with the **base** of the shoot covered, leaving the tip exposed, shows that it is the covering of the tip and not the covering itself that matters. Keep the species and age of the seedlings, the temperature, the water and the light intensity the same, use several seedlings in each set, and after two or three days measure the **direction and angle** each shoot has bent. Expected results: intact shoots and base-covered shoots **bend towards the light**; capped shoots and tipless shoots **grow straight**, and the tipless ones grow little. Explanation: the **tip** makes **auxin**, which moves to the **shaded side** of the shoot and makes the cells there **elongate** more, so the shoot curves towards the light. A cap stops light reaching the tip, so the auxin is spread evenly and the shoot grows straight; without a tip there is little auxin at all.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): a simple method, such as lighting seedlings from one side and seeing whether they bend, or a bare statement that auxin makes shoots bend towards light, with little comparison or control

Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a workable method with one-sided light and at least two sets, such as intact and capped tips, with some controlled variables and the expected results, and a partial auxin explanation, such as auxin moving to the shaded side, but a gap in either the method or the explanation

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a full method with one-sided light, sets with intact tips, capped tips and a control for the covering (base covered or a clear cap), controlled variables, several seedlings per set and a measured outcome; the expected results, intact and control shoots bending and capped ones growing straight; and a full explanation that the tip makes auxin, which moves to the shaded side where cells elongate more, and that a cap leaves the auxin evenly spread

criteria.text: Grows sets of similar seedlings in a box lit from one side only, for a set time
Compares tips left intact, tips covered with light-proof caps, and a control for the covering (the base covered instead, or a transparent cap); a set with the tips removed may also be included
Keeps other variables the same, such as species and age of seedling, temperature, water and light intensity, and uses several seedlings in each set
Measures the outcome: the direction and angle of bending of each shoot after the set time
Gives the expected results: intact shoots bend towards the light, while capped shoots and shoots without tips grow straight (and tipless shoots grow little)

Explains the results: the tip produces auxin, which moves to the shaded side and makes the cells there elongate more, so the shoot bends; a cap stops light reaching the tip so the auxin stays evenly spread and the shoot grows straight

questions.modelAnswer:
**Method.** Grow sets of seedlings of the same species, planted at the same time, in pots in a box that is dark except for a window on one side, so that light reaches them from **one direction only**. Treat the sets differently: leave the tips of the first set **intact**; cover the tips of the second set with small **light-proof foil caps**; **cut off** the tips of the third set; and cover the **base** of the fourth set with a foil sleeve, leaving the tip exposed, to show that it is covering the tip, not the foil itself, that matters. Use at least five seedlings in each set, so that one odd seedling does not decide the result.

**Variables.** The independent variable is what is done to the tip. The dependent variable is the response: after two or three days, measure the **angle** each shoot has bent from the vertical with a protractor, and note the direction. Keep everything else the same: temperature, the amount of water given, the light intensity at the window, and the length of time the seedlings are left.

**Expected results.** The intact shoots and the base-covered shoots **bend towards the light**. The capped shoots **grow straight** upwards, and the shoots with no tip grow straight too, and grow very little.

**Explanation.** The **tip** of the shoot makes the hormone **auxin**, which moves down into the cells behind it and makes them **elongate**. When light comes from one side, the auxin moves to the **shaded side**, so the cells there elongate more than those on the lit side, and the shoot curves towards the light. If the tip is covered, no light reaches the place where the direction is detected, so the auxin stays **evenly spread** and both sides grow equally: a straight shoot. If the tip is removed there is little auxin at all, so there is little elongation and no bending. Covering the base changes nothing, because the tip can still detect the light and the auxin still reaches the cells below. Together the four sets show that the tip, and only the tip, detects where the light is.

examTechnique.body: All of this is Biology-only content. The adaptations and hormones (6.14B to 6.16B) are Topic 6, so Paper 2; the plant defences (5.9B and 5.10B) are Topic 5, so Paper 1. Adaptation questions are "explain how" with feature-to-function pairs. Hormone questions test where auxin is made, where it collects and what it does, and the difference between shoots and roots. Uses of hormones are evaluated: benefit, drawback, judgement.
examinerErrors: Saying the shoot "grows towards the light" without explaining the uneven growth caused by auxin.
Forgetting that auxin inhibits elongation in roots.
Calling a poison a physical defence.
Naming the wrong hormone for ripening: it is ethene, not auxin.
Giving only advantages when asked to evaluate a commercial use.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer applies surface area, the water vapour gradient and oxygen supply to a plant it has never seen, explains tropisms as uneven growth driven by where auxin collects, keeps the shoot and root responses straight, and evaluates hormone use with a benefit, a drawback and a conclusion.
